faq.title: Frequently Asked Questions
faq.q1: What is friction rate in HVAC duct sizing?
faq.a1: Friction rate is the pressure drop per 100 feet of duct length, measured in inches of water gauge (in/wg). It determines how much resistance air encounters as it flows through the ductwork. A typical residential supply duct uses 0.08 in/wg per 100 ft.
faq.q2: What is the difference between metal and flex ducts?
faq.a2: Metal ducts are rigid, durable, and provide lower friction loss due to their smooth interior surface. Flex ducts are flexible, easier to install, but have a corrugated interior that creates more air resistance, typically adding about 50% more equivalent length for bends.
faq.q3: How do I calculate Total Equivalent Length (TEL)?
faq.a3: TEL is the sum of the actual duct length plus the equivalent lengths of all fittings (bends, transitions, tees). Each fitting type adds a specific equivalent length. For example, a 90° bend in metal duct adds approximately 10 feet of equivalent length.
faq.q4: What duct size do I need for a given CFM?
faq.a4: The required duct size depends on the desired airflow (CFM) and the allowable friction rate. Use our calculator by selecting 'CFM (Airflow)' in the 'Enter either' dropdown, input your airflow and friction rate, and the calculator will determine the required duct diameter.
faq.q5: How do I convert rectangular ducts to round equivalents?
faq.a5: Use the ASHRAE formula: De = 1.3 × (a×b)^0.625 / (a+b)^0.25, where a and b are the rectangular duct dimensions. Our converter tool below the main calculator does this calculation instantly.
faq.q6: What is a good velocity for residential ductwork?
faq.a6: For residential supply ducts, the recommended velocity is typically 600-900 feet per minute (FPM). Return ducts can be slightly higher at 600-700 FPM. Exceeding these velocities can cause noise issues.

about.title: About HVAC Duct Calculator
about.description: Learn about our free HVAC duct sizing tool built for HVAC professionals and contractors.
about.content1: HVAC Duct Calculator is a professional-grade digital tool designed to help HVAC engineers, contractors, and home performance technicians calculate accurate ductwork sizing. Our mission is to provide an accessible, reliable, and free alternative to complex engineering software for day-to-day HVAC design and troubleshooting.
about.content2: All calculations provided by this tool are based on established industry standards, primarily the equal friction method and ASHRAE (American Society of Heating, Refrigerating and Air-Conditioning Engineers) guidelines. We utilize the Darcy-Weisbach equation and standard air density assumptions to ensure engineering accuracy for both metal and flexible ductwork systems.
about.content3: This tool was created to help professionals quickly verify branch and trunk sizes, estimate pressure losses, and ensure systems operate within recommended velocity limits. While our calculator is highly accurate for planning, it is designed to complement—not replace—a full Manual D duct design performed by a licensed professional.

hub.snippet: Enter CFM, friction rate, velocity, duct type, and TEL to calculate round or rectangular HVAC duct size. Includes CFM charts, flex duct sizing, and pressure loss.
hub.s1.title: What Is an HVAC Duct Calculator
hub.s1.p1: An HVAC duct calculator (also called a ductulator or duct size calculator) is a tool used to determine the correct duct dimensions for heating, ventilation, and air conditioning systems. It takes inputs such as airflow in CFM, friction loss rate, duct length, and the number of fittings to calculate the ideal duct diameter or rectangular equivalent.
hub.s1.p2: Professional HVAC engineers and contractors rely on duct sizing calculators to ensure systems deliver the right amount of conditioned air to each room. Without accurate sizing, systems waste energy, create uncomfortable hot or cold spots, and generate unwanted noise.
hub.s2.title: How to Use the Duct Calculator
hub.s2.p1: Using our free HVAC duct calculator is simple. Follow these steps to calculate your duct size accurately:
hub.s2.step1: Select your duct type (metal or flex) at the top of the calculator.
hub.s2.step2: Choose whether to size by friction rate or velocity. For residential systems, friction rate (0.08 in/wg per 100 ft) is the standard method.
hub.s2.step3: Enter your Total Effective Length (TEL), which includes the actual duct run plus equivalent lengths for all bends and fittings.
hub.s2.step4: Enter either your known duct size or your required CFM airflow.
hub.s2.step5: Click Calculate to see your results including CFM, velocity, pressure loss, and recommended duct dimensions.
hub.s3.title: Duct Sizing Formula Explained
hub.s3.p1: The core formula used in HVAC duct sizing is based on the Darcy Weisbach equation and ASHRAE equal friction method. For round ducts, the relationship between airflow, duct size, and friction rate is:
hub.s3.formula1desc: Where Q is airflow in CFM, A is the cross sectional area of the duct in square feet, and V is velocity in feet per minute (FPM).
hub.s3.p2: For a round duct, the area is calculated as A = π × (D/2)² where D is the diameter in feet. The friction rate determines how much static pressure is lost per 100 feet of duct run.
hub.s3.p3: For example, an 8 inch round duct at 700 FPM velocity delivers approximately 244 CFM of airflow. This is the standard capacity used in most residential branch duct runs.
hub.s4.title: Understanding Airflow CFM in HVAC
hub.s4.p1: CFM stands for Cubic Feet per Minute and measures the volume of air flowing through a duct. Every room in a building requires a specific amount of airflow to maintain comfort. The required CFM depends on the room size, heat load (BTU), and the system design.
hub.s4.p2: A general rule of thumb for residential HVAC is 1 CFM per square foot of floor area. For cooling, the typical requirement is 400 CFM per ton of cooling capacity. One ton of cooling equals 12,000 BTU per hour.
hub.s4.formuladesc: Where BTU is the heating or cooling load and ΔT is the temperature difference between supply and return air (typically 20°F for cooling).
hub.s5.title: Friction Rate and Static Pressure Explained
hub.s5.p1: Friction rate is the pressure drop that occurs per 100 feet of duct length, measured in inches of water gauge (in/wg). As air moves through ductwork, it loses energy due to friction against the duct walls. The smoother the duct interior, the lower the friction loss.
hub.s5.p2: Static pressure is the total resistance that the blower fan must overcome to push air through the entire duct system. It includes friction losses in straight duct runs, pressure drops across fittings, and losses through filters, coils, and registers.
hub.s5.p3: For residential supply ducts, the standard friction rate is 0.08 in/wg per 100 feet. Commercial systems may use rates from 0.08 to 0.60 in/wg depending on the application and available static pressure from the air handler.
hub.s6.title: How to Calculate Total Effective Length
hub.s6.p1: Total Effective Length (TEL) is a critical value in duct sizing. It represents the total resistance path that air must travel, combining the actual straight duct length with the equivalent lengths of all fittings such as elbows, tees, transitions, and takeoffs.
hub.s6.p2: Each fitting adds resistance equivalent to a certain length of straight duct. Common equivalent lengths for metal ductwork include:
hub.s6.fitting4: Branch takeoff: 25 to 35 feet equivalent length
hub.s6.formula: TEL = Straight Length + Σ(Fitting Equivalent Lengths)
hub.s6.p3: For flex duct, multiply the equivalent lengths by 1.5 because the corrugated interior creates significantly more friction than smooth metal duct.
hub.s7.title: Common Duct Sizing Mistakes
hub.s7.p1: Incorrect duct sizing is one of the most frequent problems in HVAC installations. Here are the mistakes that professionals and DIY installers make most often:
hub.s7.m1d: Ducts that are too small restrict airflow, increase velocity and noise, raise static pressure, and force the blower to work harder. This leads to higher energy bills and reduced equipment lifespan.
hub.s7.m2d: Ducts that are too large waste materials and reduce air velocity below the minimum needed for proper air distribution. Low velocity can cause temperature stratification where warm air rises and cool air settles.
hub.s7.m3d: Many installers only measure the straight duct run and forget to add equivalent lengths for elbows, tees, and other fittings. This can underestimate the total resistance by 30% to 50%.
hub.s7.m4d: Applying commercial friction rates to residential systems (or vice versa) leads to improper sizing. Always use the friction rate appropriate for your application type.
hub.s8.title: Duct Material Impact on Airflow
hub.s8.p1: The material and construction of your ductwork significantly affect airflow performance, friction losses, and overall system efficiency. The two most common duct types are sheet metal and flexible duct.
hub.s8.p2: Sheet metal ducts have smooth interior surfaces that minimize friction loss. They are the preferred choice for main trunk lines and any run where low pressure drop is important. Metal ducts also seal better, reducing air leakage.
hub.s8.p3: Flexible ducts are made of a wire helix wrapped in plastic and insulation. They are easier and faster to install but create significantly more friction due to their corrugated interior. When using flex duct, increase your equivalent lengths by 50% and keep runs as short and straight as possible. Avoid sharp bends and compression, as these dramatically increase resistance.
hub.s9.title: Why Accurate Duct Sizing Matters
hub.s9.p1: Proper duct sizing is the foundation of an efficient, comfortable, and quiet HVAC system. When ducts are sized correctly, the system delivers the right amount of air to each room at acceptable noise levels while operating at peak efficiency.
hub.s9.p2: Poorly sized ductwork causes a chain reaction of problems: uneven temperatures between rooms, excessive noise from high velocity air, increased energy consumption as the blower works harder, premature equipment failure, and reduced indoor air quality from improper air circulation.
hub.s9.p3: Studies show that improperly sized duct systems can increase energy consumption by 20% to 40%. For a typical home spending $2,000 per year on heating and cooling, that translates to $400 to $800 in wasted energy costs annually.

hub.reviewed.author: Verified HVAC Engineering Calculations
hub.reviewed.disclaimer: Disclaimer: This calculator provides estimates for educational and planning purposes. Actual duct sizing should be verified by a licensed HVAC professional using Manual J (load calculation) and Manual D (duct design) procedures. Local building codes and specific equipment requirements may affect final duct sizing.
faq.q7: How do I calculate duct size based on room square footage?
faq.a7: First, determine the CFM needed for the room using the rule of 1 CFM per square foot. For example, a 200 square foot room needs approximately 200 CFM. Then use a duct sizing calculator with your friction rate (typically 0.08 in/wg) to find the required duct diameter. A 200 CFM requirement typically needs an 8 inch round duct.
faq.q8: What is Manual J and why does it matter for duct sizing?
faq.a8: Manual J is the ACCA (Air Conditioning Contractors of America) standard procedure for calculating heating and cooling loads for buildings. It determines exactly how many BTU each room needs based on factors like insulation, windows, orientation, and climate zone. Manual J results feed directly into duct sizing because they determine the CFM airflow required for each room.
faq.q9: What is Manual D in HVAC?
faq.a9: Manual D is the ACCA standard for residential duct design. It provides the procedure for sizing duct systems based on the airflow requirements from Manual J. Manual D accounts for available static pressure, duct layout, fitting losses, and equipment specifications to determine the correct duct size for each run in the system.
faq.q10: What is static pressure in HVAC systems?
faq.a10: Static pressure is the resistance to airflow in a duct system, measured in inches of water gauge (in/wg). Think of it as the air pressure that the blower fan must generate to push air through all the ductwork, fittings, filters, coils, and registers. A typical residential system operates at 0.5 in/wg total external static pressure.
faq.q11: How do I convert BTU to tonnage for HVAC systems?
faq.a11: One ton of cooling capacity equals 12,000 BTU per hour. To convert BTU to tons, simply divide the BTU value by 12,000. For example, a 36,000 BTU system equals 3 tons (36,000 ÷ 12,000 = 3). Each ton of cooling requires approximately 400 CFM of airflow.
faq.q12: What is the difference between a ductulator and a duct calculator?
faq.a12: A ductulator is a traditional circular slide rule tool used by HVAC professionals to look up duct sizes based on CFM and friction rate. A duct calculator is the digital version that performs the same calculations automatically. Our online HVAC duct calculator provides the same results as a physical ductulator but with added features like rectangular to round conversion and automatic TEL calculations.
faq.q13: Can I use this calculator for commercial HVAC systems?
faq.a13: Yes, this calculator works for both residential and commercial duct sizing. For commercial systems, use the appropriate friction rate for your application (typically 0.08 to 0.60 in/wg per 100 feet) and ensure you account for higher airflow volumes and longer duct runs typical in commercial buildings.
faq.q14: What causes noise in HVAC duct systems?
faq.a14: Duct noise is primarily caused by excessive air velocity. When air moves too fast through ductwork, it creates turbulence that produces a rushing or whistling sound. The main causes include undersized ducts, sharp bends without turning vanes, improperly supported flex duct, and loose connections. Keeping velocity below 900 FPM in residential supply ducts minimizes noise.
faq.q15: How does wrong duct sizing affect energy costs?
faq.a15: Incorrectly sized ducts force the HVAC blower to work harder to maintain airflow, which increases electrical consumption. Undersized ducts create high static pressure that reduces blower efficiency. Oversized ducts reduce air velocity and cause poor distribution, leading to some rooms being too hot or too cold. Both scenarios can increase energy bills by 20% to 40% compared to a properly sized system.
hub.s10a.title: Understanding Calculator Inputs
hub.s10a.p1: Each input field in our HVAC duct calculator controls a specific aspect of the sizing calculation. Understanding what each field means helps you enter accurate values and get reliable results.
hub.s10a.ducttype: Duct Type: Select metal (galvanized steel) or flex (flexible duct). Metal ducts have smooth interior walls and lower friction loss. Flex ducts have corrugated interiors that increase friction by approximately 50%. The calculator automatically adjusts friction calculations based on your selection.
hub.s10a.method: Sizing Method: Choose between friction rate (standard approach) and velocity (noise focused approach). Friction rate is recommended for most residential and commercial designs. Velocity method is used when noise control is the primary concern.
hub.s10a.frictionrate: Friction Rate: The allowable pressure drop per 100 feet of duct, measured in inches of water gauge (in/wg). Residential supply ducts typically use 0.08 in/wg per 100 ft. Lower values produce larger, quieter ducts. Higher values allow smaller ducts but increase noise and energy use.
hub.s10a.tel: Total Effective Length (TEL): The combined resistance of your duct run in equivalent feet. It includes the straight duct length plus equivalent lengths for all fittings (bends, transitions, takeoffs). Our calculator lets you enter the straight length and number of bends separately.
hub.s10a.bends: Bend Counts: Enter the number of 45 degree, 90 degree, and 180 degree bends in the duct run. Each bend adds equivalent length: 5 feet for 45 degree, 10 feet for 90 degree, and 20 feet for 180 degree bends. For flex duct, these values are automatically multiplied by 1.5.
hub.s10a.dimensions: Duct Dimensions: Enter either the known duct size or the required CFM airflow. If you enter a duct diameter, the calculator tells you the CFM capacity. If you enter a CFM requirement, it calculates the needed duct size.
hub.s10b.title: What Your Results Mean
hub.s10b.p1: After clicking calculate, the tool displays several output values. Each one tells you something important about how the duct will perform in your system.
hub.s10b.cfm: CFM (Cubic Feet per Minute): The volume of air flowing through the duct each minute. This must match the airflow requirement of the room or zone the duct serves. Typical residential rooms need 100 to 400 CFM depending on size.
hub.s10b.velocity: Velocity (FPM): The speed of air moving through the duct in feet per minute. For quiet residential operation, keep velocity below 900 FPM for supply ducts and below 700 FPM for return ducts. Higher velocities cause audible noise.
hub.s10b.pressloss: Pressure Loss (in/wg): The total static pressure drop across the duct run. This value must not exceed the available static pressure from your blower fan. If pressure loss is too high, the duct is undersized or the run is too long.
hub.s10b.ductsize: Recommended Duct Size: The minimum duct diameter (round) or dimensions (rectangular) needed to deliver the required airflow at acceptable velocity and pressure loss. Always round up to the next standard duct size available from your supplier.
hub.s10b.noiselevel: Noise Assessment: Based on the calculated velocity, the tool indicates whether the duct will operate quietly, at moderate noise, or at potentially noisy levels. For bedrooms and offices, aim for the quiet range.
hub.s10c.title: Real World Use Cases
hub.s10c.p1: Our HVAC duct calculator is designed for professionals and homeowners working on real projects. Here are the most common scenarios where accurate duct sizing makes the difference.
hub.s10c.uc1d: When building a new home, every duct must be sized from scratch. Use the calculator to size trunk lines, branch runs, and return ducts for each room based on the Manual J load calculation. Getting it right during construction avoids expensive modifications later.
hub.s10c.uc2d: Extending ductwork to a new room requires calculating whether the existing trunk can handle additional airflow. Use the calculator to verify the trunk capacity and size the new branch duct for the added room's CFM requirement.
hub.s10c.uc3d: During renovation, verify that existing duct sizes actually match the airflow needs of each room. Many older homes have undersized ducts. Use the calculator to check whether current duct sizes deliver adequate CFM at acceptable velocity.
hub.s10c.uc4d: If certain rooms are always too hot or too cold, the duct serving that room may be undersized. Measure the duct diameter, enter it with the room's CFM requirement, and check if the velocity exceeds 900 FPM. If it does, the duct needs to be larger.
